title: CPU Execution & Control
summary: The control unit is the CPU's conductor. Learn how it drives execution, single-cycle vs multi-cycle, and hardwired vs microprogrammed control.

blocks.markdown:
The **control unit** is the part of the CPU that decides what happens on every clock tick — which parts turn on, in what order.

- It reads the current instruction and drives everything else: [cpu-datapath](cpu-datapath).
- Two build styles exist: **hardwired** and **microprogrammed**.
- Execution can run in **one cycle** or **many cycles** per instruction — a core trade-off.
- **Architecture** (what an ISA promises) is different from **microarchitecture** (how a chip delivers it).

The control unit doesn't compute results — it **orchestrates**. Every cycle it looks at the current instruction (and often which step it's on) and asks: which units should act now?

- It never touches data directly; it only tells other units what to do.
- Its output is a set of **control signals** — the switches that turn the rest of the CPU on and off.
- Without it, the ALU, registers, and memory would have no idea when to act.

A **control signal** is a single wire the control unit sets to 0 or 1 to switch a specific piece of hardware on or off.

- **RegWrite** — allowed to write into the register file?
- **MemRead / MemWrite** — read or write memory this cycle?
- **ALUOp** — which operation should the ALU perform?
- **PCSrc** — where should the next address come from?

One instruction usually sets several of these together, each cycle.

Trace an `ADD` instruction through the control unit.

- **Fetch** — control raises signals to read memory at the PC and load the instruction register.
- **Decode** — control reads the opcode and sets ALUOp to "add".
- **Execute** — control enables the ALU and register read ports.
- **Writeback** — control raises RegWrite so the sum lands in the destination register.

Each step is just a different set of signals turned on.

blocks.subTitle: Single-cycle
blocks.markdown:
In a **single-cycle** design, every instruction finishes in exactly one clock cycle, no matter how simple or complex.

- Control logic is simple — one fixed set of signals per instruction type.
- The cycle must be as long as the **slowest** instruction (e.g. a memory load), wasting time on fast ones.
- Hardware for every stage (fetch, ALU, memory) must exist separately, since it all fires at once.

blocks.subTitle: Multi-cycle
blocks.markdown:
In a **multi-cycle** design, an instruction is broken into steps (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback), and each step takes one shorter cycle.

- Simple instructions skip unneeded steps and finish sooner; the clock can run faster overall.
- Hardware like the ALU can be **reused** across steps instead of duplicated.
- Cost: control is harder — it must track which step an instruction is on.

blocks.subTitle: Side by side
blocks.markdown:
The trade-off in one view.

| | Single-cycle | Multi-cycle |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle length | Fixed, worst-case | Short, uniform |
| Hardware reuse | None | ALU, memory reused |
| Control logic | Simple | Tracks current step |

Multi-cycle also sets up the idea behind **pipelining** — see [pipelining](pipelining).

**CPI (cycles per instruction)** is the average number of clock cycles an instruction takes to finish.

- Single-cycle designs: CPI is always **1**, but the cycle itself is long.
- Multi-cycle designs: CPI **varies** by instruction (e.g. 3 for ADD, 5 for a load), but each cycle is short.
- Total time = instructions × CPI × cycle time — a lower CPI doesn't always mean faster.

blocks.subTitle: Hardwired control
blocks.markdown:
**Hardwired control** builds the control unit out of fixed logic gates that map instruction bits directly to control signals.

- Very fast — signals appear as soon as the gates settle.
- Rigid: adding or changing an instruction means redesigning the circuit.
- Common in simple or performance-critical designs (classic RISC chips).

blocks.subTitle: Microprogrammed control
blocks.markdown:
**Microprogrammed control** stores the control signals as tiny instructions — **microcode** — in an internal memory, one microinstruction per step.

- Each machine instruction points to a short sequence of microcode that raises the right signals in order.
- Easy to fix bugs or add instructions: edit the microcode, not the circuit.
- Slower than hardwired, since it adds a memory lookup per step. Used in CISC chips like x86.

blocks.subTitle: Side by side
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to generate the same signals.

| | Hardwired | Microprogrammed |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Faster | Slower (extra lookup) |
| Flexibility | Fixed at design time | Change microcode, not circuit |
| Typical use | RISC, simple cores | CISC, complex instruction sets |

The **architecture** is the **ISA** — the contract of instructions, registers, and behavior a programmer can rely on: [instruction-set-architecture](instruction-set-architecture).

- The **microarchitecture** is one specific way to *implement* that contract in hardware — single-cycle or multi-cycle, hardwired or microprogrammed, with or without pipelining.
- Same architecture, many microarchitectures: two x86 chips run the same programs but differ completely inside.
- This split is why software rarely needs to change when a chip is redesigned.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Lower CPI always means faster."** Not if the cycle time is longer — total time is what matters.
- **"Microcode is just software."** It's still hardware-level signal control, just stored in memory instead of gates.
- **"Architecture and microarchitecture are the same thing."** One's the promise, the other's the implementation — they change independently.

blocks.subTitle: What does the control unit do
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does the control unit actually do?**

It generates the control signals that tell every other part of the CPU — ALU, registers, memory — what to do each cycle. It doesn't process data itself; it decides the sequence and timing of everything that does.

blocks.subTitle: Single-cycle vs multi-cycle
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why not just make every CPU single-cycle — isn't CPI of 1 the best?**

Because the cycle length has to fit the slowest instruction, so simple instructions waste time waiting. Multi-cycle designs run a much shorter clock and let simple instructions finish sooner, so total execution time usually wins even though CPI rises above 1.

blocks.subTitle: Hardwired vs microprogrammed
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Hardwired vs microprogrammed control — how do you choose?**

Hardwired if speed matters most and the instruction set is small and stable — it's pure logic gates with no lookup delay. Microprogrammed if the instruction set is large or likely to change — you patch microcode in memory instead of redesigning circuits.

blocks.subTitle: Architecture vs microarchitecture
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between architecture and microarchitecture?**

Architecture (the ISA) is the visible contract — instructions, registers, behavior — that software is written against. Microarchitecture is how a specific chip implements that contract internally. Two chips can share an architecture yet have completely different microarchitectures.
